    28	I. INTRODUCTION
    29	“The hardest thing in the world to understand is income tax!” – Albert Einstein
    30	
    31	Taxes are complicated. The U.S. federal tax code contains over three million words –
    32	about 6,000 pages. A casual browsing of the tax code’s table of contents offers a glimpse
    33	into the vast complexity of federal taxation. Entire sections of the tax code apply
    34	specifically to the taxation of vaccines (Sec. 4131-4132), shipowners' mutual protection
    35	and indemnity associations (Sec. 526), specially sweetened natural wines (Sec. 5385),
    36	and life insurance companies (Sec. 801-818). Annual changes to the tax code imply that
    37	taxes will continue to become more complex even as politicians tout tax simplification.
    38	Taxes levied by other jurisdictions, such as states and cities, add further complexity to
    39	taxation in the U.S. Americans spend billions of hours each year working on their taxes,
    40	not to mention the costs of accountants and tax preparers.
    41	Fortunately, one needn’t comprehend the imposing complexity of the tax code to
    42	understand the crucial role of taxes in American society. Taxation is an important, but
    43	commonly neglected, topic for students of economics, political science, and other
    44	disciplines. Tax policy has important economic consequences, both for the national
    45	economy and for particular groups within the economy. Tax policies are often designed
    46	with the intention of stimulating economic growth – although economists differ
    47	drastically about which policies are most effective at fostering growth. Taxes can create
    48	incentives promoting desirable behavior and disincentives for unwanted behavior.
    49	Taxation provides a means to redistribute economic resources towards those with low
    50	incomes or special needs. Taxes provide the revenue needed for critical public services
    51	such as social security, health care, national defense, and education.
    52	Taxation is as much of a political issue as an economic issue. Political leaders have used
    53	tax policy to promote their agendas by initiating various tax reforms: decreasing (or
    54	increasing) tax rates, changing the definition of taxable income, creating new taxes on
    55	specific products, etc. Of course, no one particularly wants to pay taxes. Specific
    56	groups, such as small-business owners, farmers, or retired individuals, exert significant
    57	political effort to reduce their share of the tax burden. The voluminous tax code is
    58	packed with rules that benefit a certain group of taxpayers while inevitably shifting more
    59	of the burden to others. Tax policy clearly reflects the expression of power in the U.S. –
    60	those without power or favor are left paying more in taxes while others reap the benefits
    61	of lower taxes because of their political influence. Broad attempts to reform the tax
    62	system have produced dramatic and sudden shifts in tax policy, generally motivated by
    63	political factors rather than sound economic theory. For example, the top marginal
    64	federal tax bracket on individual income in the U.S. dropped precipitously from 70% to
    65	28% during the 1980s. Tax policy has clearly been used to promote political, as well as
    66	economic, agendas.
    67	This module is intended to provide a basic understanding of the economic, political, and
    68	social context of the entire U.S. tax system. When most people think about taxes, they
    69	1
    70	
    71	
    72	tend to think only of the federal income tax. However, looking solely at the federal
    73	income tax would miss several important issues. Perhaps most importantly, the federal
    74	income tax is not the largest tax bill to most Americans. We’ll see that the largest tax for
    75	most Americans is federal social insurance taxation. Also, the federal income tax is one
    76	of the most progressive taxes in the U.S. system. When all taxes are considered, the U.S.
    77	tax system is much less progressive. You may be surprised to find out how many taxes in
    78	the U.S. are actually regressive – hitting low-income households at a disproportionately
    79	high rate.
    80	This module is divided into three major sections. First, some basic terms will be defined
    81	and discussed, including tax progressivity and the differences between several types of
    82	taxes. Second, a brief overview of tax history in the United States will be presented.
    83	Third, data on tax trends will be used to illustrate the changing nature of taxation with a
    84	focus on the overall progressivity of the entire tax system.
    85	
    86	II. THE STRUCTURE OF TAXATION IN THE UNITED STATES
    87	Tax Progressivity
    88	The overall system of taxation in the United States is progressive. By a progressive tax
    89	system, we mean that the percentage of income an individual (or household) pays in taxes
    90	tends to increase with increasing income. Not only do those with higher incomes pay
    91	more in total taxes, they pay a higher rate of taxes. This is the essence of a progressive
    92	tax system. For example, a person making $100,000 in a year might pay 25% of their
    93	income in taxes ($25,000 in taxes), while someone with an income of $30,000 might only
    94	pay a 10% tax rate ($3,000 in taxes).
    95	A tax system may also be regressive or proportional. A regressive tax system is one
    96	where the proportion of income paid in taxes tends to decrease as one’s income increases.
    97	A proportional tax system simply means that everyone pays the same tax rate regardless
    98	of income. A particular tax system may display elements of more than one approach.
    99	Consider a hypothetical tax system where one pays a proportional, or flat 1 , rate on
   100	income below a certain dollar amount and then progressively increasing rates above that
   101	dollar amount. Also, within an overall tax system, some particular taxes might be
   102	progressive while other taxes are regressive. We’ll see later on that this the case in the
   103	United States.
   104	The Reasons for Progressive Taxation
   105	The overall tax system of the United States, and in most other countries, is progressive
   106	for a number of reasons. A progressive tax embodies the concept that those with high
   107	incomes should pay more of their income in taxes because of their greater ability to pay

   113	Thus, the
   114	flat tax proposals would retain a small degree of progressivity.

   531	III. A BRIEF HISTORY OF TAXATION IN THE U.S. 10
   532	Before the Federal Income Tax
   533	The tax mechanisms used during first 150 years or so of U.S. tax history bears little
   534	resemblance to the current system of taxation. First, the U.S. Constitution restricted
   535	“direct” taxation by the federal government – meaning taxes directly on individuals.
   536	Instead, the federal government relied on indirect taxes including taxes on imports
   537	(tariffs) and excise taxes. Tariffs were the major source of U.S. government receipts
   538	from the beginning of the nation up to the early 1900’s. For example, in 1800 custom
   539	duties comprised about 84% of government receipts (U.S. Census Bureau, 1960).
   540	Internal federal revenue collections (which exclude tariffs on imports) as recently as the
   541	early 20th century were primarily derived from excise taxes on alcohol. In 1900 over
   542	60% of internal revenue collections came from alcohol excise taxes with another 20%
   543	from tobacco excise taxes.
   544	Another important difference is the scale of government taxation and expenditures
   545	relative to the entire economy. Government spending is currently a major portion of the
   546	total U.S. economy – in 2010 government expenditures and investment at all levels
   547	comprised about 20% of total economic output. In the late 1800s government
   548	expenditures were responsible for only about 2% of national output (earlier data on
   549	national output are not available). The role of government has become more prominent
   550	as a result of expansion of military activity and an increase in the provision of public
   551	services. Consequently an overall trend of increasing taxation is evident, although we’ll
   552	see that this trend has recently stabilized or reversed.
   553	The Constitutional framers were wary of a government’s power to tax. Taxation of the
   554	American Colonies by a distant and corrupt England was a driving force behind the
   555	American Revolution. Consequently, they believed in decentralized taxation and
   556	delegated most public revenue collection to localities, which relied primarily on property
   557	taxes. During peacetime the federal government was able to meet its expenses through
   558	relatively modest excise taxes and tariffs. During times of war, such as the War of 1812,
   559	federal taxes were temporarily raised to finance the war or pay down the ensuing debts.
   560	Once the financial crisis passed, taxes were reduced in response to public opposition to
   561	high tax rates.
   562	Like previous wars, the Civil War initiated an increase in both excise tax and tariff rates.
   563	Government revenue collections increased by a factor of seven between 1863 and 1866.
   564	Perhaps the most significant tax policy enacted during the Civil War was the institution
   565	of the first national income tax. Concerns about the legality of the tax, considering the
   566	Constitution’s prohibition of direct taxation, were muted during the national emergency.
   567	The income tax rates were low by modern standards – a maximum rate of 10% along
   568	with generous exemptions meant that only about 10% of households were subject to any
   569	income tax. Still, the income tax generated over 20% of federal revenues in 1865. After

   582	The Populists revived interest in an income tax as a means to introduce a progressive tax

   584	concentration of wealth and power. In other words, the tax was not envisioned as a

   592	While the initial income tax was progressive, it was less radical than many desired. In

**Before the federal income tax**
- The U.S. Constitution restricted "direct" federal taxation (taxes directly on individuals), so the federal government relied on indirect taxes: tariffs on imports and excise taxes. Tariffs were the major source of government receipts from the founding of the nation into the early 1900s — in 1800, customs duties were about 84% of government receipts. As late as 1900, over 60% of internal revenue collections came from alcohol excise taxes and another 20% from tobacco.
- The framers, wary of the power to tax (taxation of the colonies by England had driven the Revolution), favored decentralized taxation, delegating most revenue collection to localities that relied primarily on property taxes. In peacetime, modest excise taxes and tariffs sufficed; in wartime (e.g., the War of 1812), taxes were temporarily raised and then cut after public opposition.
- Government was small relative to the economy: in the late 1800s government expenditures were only about 2% of national output, versus about 20% in 2010.
- The Civil War raised excise and tariff rates (revenue collections rose sevenfold between 1863 and 1866) and produced the first national income tax. With a maximum rate of 10% and generous exemptions, only about 10% of households paid it, yet it generated over 20% of federal revenues in 1865. Few politicians favored keeping it, and it expired in 1872.
- The Populist movement of the late 1800s revived the income tax as a progressive, ability-to-pay vehicle of social justice (a response to monopoly profits and concentrated wealth), not mainly as a revenue source. A federal income tax with a $4,000 exemption was instituted in 1894, but the Supreme Court ruled it unconstitutional in 1895. After failed amendment attempts, the 16th Amendment was ratified in 1913, creating the legal basis for the federal income tax. The initial tax was progressive but mild — only about 2% of households paid it, at rates of just 1%–7%.

**The growth of direct taxation (WWI–WWII)**
- World War I transformed the income tax: the top marginal rate jumped from 7% in 1915 to 67% in 1917; corporate taxes became a major revenue source (over a quarter of internal revenue in 1917); and the estate tax was created in 1916 as an instrument of progressive taxation.
- Unlike after earlier wars, much of the WWI tax system remained. Tariffs fell from about half of government receipts in 1910 to under 15% by 1925, while corporate and individual income taxes made up nearly half of receipts in the mid-1920s. Excise collections dropped sharply, especially during Prohibition.
- The Great Depression cut federal receipts; rates were raised in 1932. FDR made progressive taxation a key element of the New Deal, but the most significant measure was old-age insurance (Social Security), funded by a separate tax split equally between employers and employees (initially 2%, 1% each) — a design that protected it from political attack.
- World War II produced the most dramatic shift. FDR sought to tax corporations and high incomes heavily (he proposed capping net income after taxes at $25,000, but lacked Congressional support). The compromise halved personal exemptions between 1939 and 1942, so the income tax reached the middle class for the first time; the top rate applied to income as low as $200,000 by 1942 (down from $5 million in 1941), and the top marginal rate hit a record 94% in 1944. Payroll withholding was introduced. Individual taxpayers grew from 3.9 million in 1939 to 42.6 million in 1945, and federal income tax collections leaped from $2.2 billion to $35.1 billion. By the end of the war, nearly 90% of the labor force filed returns and about 60% paid income taxes; federal income tax's share of all taxes collected rose from 16% in 1940 to over 51% by 1950.
- After WWII, much of this structure remained, with both parties supporting a progressive but broad income tax, relatively flat corporate rates, and regressive social insurance taxes.

**From the "Reagan Revolution" to the Bush tax cuts**
- Changes between the end of WWII and the 1980s were generally minor: the Social Security tax rose from 2% to 6.13% by 1979; Medicare and Medicaid were established in the 1960s; and the 1964 across-the-board tax cut lowered the top marginal rate from 91% (1963) to 70% (1965). Government spending grew from under 18% of GDP in 1946 to over 22% by the mid-1970s.
- The 1980s ended this stasis. Reagan's Economic Recovery Tax Act of 1981 (ERTA) enacted the largest tax cut in American history (in constant dollars), on supply-side reasoning; it phased the top rate down from 70% to 50%, cut corporate taxes, and indexed many parameters to inflation. In practice, ERTA produced the largest revenue reduction of any tax bill since WWII, and the 1982 act imposed the largest peacetime tax increase. Social Security reforms in 1983 raised its tax rates and began taxing some benefits. The Tax Reform Act of 1986 — the most comprehensive revision since the 1950s — cut the top individual rate from 50% to 28% (by 1988) and the top corporate rate from 46% to 34%. Despite the cuts, federal revenues grew nearly in line with GDP (revenues +76% vs. GDP +83% from 1980–1988); the mix shifted toward regressive social insurance taxes (up 38% of revenues), reducing overall progressivity.
- Deficits tripled during the 1980s. The first President Bush broke his "no new taxes" pledge in 1990, raising the top bracket to 31%. Clinton restored progressivity in 1993 with 36% and 39.6% brackets and a slight corporate rate increase to 35%.
- The $1.35 trillion Bush tax cut of 2001 lowered individual rates across the board (top bracket from 39.6% in 2001 to 35% by 2006), scheduled repeal of the estate tax in 2010, and expanded retirement contributions; it reduced progressivity. A 2003 cut accelerated rate decreases and lowered the top capital gains/dividends rate. The 2009 American Recovery and Reinvestment Act instituted or expanded tax credits, including a $400 payroll tax credit per worker and an expanded college tuition credit.

**Summary data trends (Section IV of the document)**
- Federal tax revenues grew considerably through the 20th century (even in inflation-adjusted terms), with the largest leap during WWII and relatively consistent growth after about 1960, punctuated by occasional declines from recessions or major tax-code changes. State and local collections grew more steadily, since they rely mainly on property and sales taxes.
- Total tax collections generally rose as a share of GDP over the 20th century; federal revenues now substantially exceed state and local revenues (a trend that began before WWII but was solidified by it). Since 2000, federal taxes as a share of GDP have declined due to recessions and rate cuts — in 2009 they were lower than in any year since the 1940s.
- The composition of federal taxation changed markedly: excise taxes dominated at the start of the century (with a Depression-era revival), corporate taxes were the most significant source from 1918–1932, and personal income taxation has since become central.

The document notes that this history is primarily derived from Brownlee (1996).
